title: Down syndrome: health needs across life
blurb: Anticipate the health needs linked to Down syndrome, from the newborn heart check to lifelong thyroid testing and early-onset dementia.
question: Martin, 47, has Down syndrome and lives in supported living. Over four months he has got lost on his usual walk to the shop, needs more prompting to shave and has lost interest in his darts club. Staff think he has dementia. What should the nurse do first?

teach.body: Down syndrome is caused by an extra copy of chromosome 21 in the body's cells (trisomy 21). Most people have standard trisomy 21; translocation and mosaic forms are less common. In plain English: one extra chromosome changes development and brings a recognisable pattern of health risks. Knowing that pattern lets nurses look for problems early instead of waiting for the person to report them.

teach.body: Hypothyroidism is common in Down syndrome and the risk rises with age, so thyroid function is tested every year for life, even after years of normal results. Untreated hypothyroidism causes slowing, tiredness, weight gain, low mood and loss of skills, and can look like dementia or depression. Whenever an adult with Down syndrome seems to be declining, check when the thyroid was last tested.
teach.cite: DSMIG thyroid guideline; Down's Syndrome Association

teach.body: Chromosome 21 carries the APP gene, which makes amyloid precursor protein. An extra copy drives amyloid plaques, and Alzheimer's changes are present in virtually all adults with Down syndrome by about 40. Early dementia often shows as changes in personality or behaviour and loss of everyday skills, more than as memory complaints. Late-onset seizures (often myoclonic jerks) are linked to the emergence of Alzheimer's disease.

teach.h: An adult with Down syndrome is losing skills

steps.label: Exclude treatable causes
steps.sub: Thyroid, hearing, sight, low mood, pain, medicines

teach.caption: NICE NG54: baseline assessment of adaptive behaviour for all adults with Down syndrome (1.7.13); dementia measures (1.7.12).
The overlap is why thyroid function and other treatable causes are checked before dementia is diagnosed.

teach.body: Martin's changes are a real decline from his baseline and must be taken seriously, but dementia is not assumed. The nurse checks his last thyroid test (it was 18 months ago), arranges thyroid bloods, hearing and sight checks, and asks about low mood, pain and any new medicines. Staff mention brief jerks of his arms in the mornings, so the nurse reports these as possible seizures. With treatable causes excluded, he is referred for dementia assessment, comparing results with his baseline.

teach.text: Two classic errors: stopping yearly thyroid tests because past results were normal (the risk rises with age), and labelling decline as dementia before excluding hypothyroidism, sensory loss and depression. NICE NG54 asks at the annual health check about change in behaviour, loss of skills or more prompting in recent months.

items: Trisomy 21: extra chromosome 21; standard, translocation and mosaic forms.
About half born with a heart condition: assess every newborn.
Thyroid test every year for life; hypothyroidism can mimic dementia.
Hearing, sight and infection risks: regular checks and flu vaccine.
Extra APP gene: early Alzheimer's; baseline for all adults; ask about change; late-onset seizures.

summary: You can now explain how trisomy 21 links to heart, thyroid, sensory, infection and dementia risks. You can plan checks across the lifespan and respond to declining skills in an adult with Down syndrome by excluding treatable causes before dementia assessment.

A.q: A student asks why people with Down syndrome develop Alzheimer's disease earlier than the general population. Which explanation is accurate?
options: A variant in the MECP2 gene on the X chromosome
An extra copy of the APP gene on chromosome 21
Loss of the maternal UBE3A gene on chromosome 15
Expanded CGG repeats in the FMR1 gene
A.why: Chromosome 21 carries the APP gene; an extra copy drives amyloid build-up, so Alzheimer's changes appear decades earlier.

whyNot.2: Loss of maternal UBE3A causes Angelman syndrome.
whyNot.3: FMR1 CGG repeat expansion causes fragile X syndrome.

A.q: Ben, 29, has Down syndrome. His mother has read that dementia is more common and asks when health checks will start to look for it. According to NHS.uk, what is the best answer?
options: From 65, in line with the general population
From 50, when memory clinics accept referrals
From about 30, because dementia occurs younger
From 40, once symptoms of memory loss appear
A.why: NHS.uk advises regular check-ups from age 30 for adults with Down syndrome because dementia tends to occur younger.

whyNot.0: Dementia occurs much earlier in Down syndrome.
whyNot.1: Waiting until 50 would miss early change.
whyNot.3: Checks look for early change before symptoms are obvious.

A.q: Sophie, 25, has Down syndrome and attends her annual health check. Which group of checks is most relevant to her syndrome?
options: Thyroid function, hearing and vision
Bone density, lipids and prostate
Liver function, iron and vitamin B12
Spirometry, peak flow and allergy tests
A.why: Hypothyroidism, hearing loss and sight problems are common in Down syndrome; thyroid testing is yearly for life.

whyNot.1: These are not the syndrome-specific priorities for a 25-year-old woman with Down syndrome.
whyNot.2: These are not routine Down syndrome checks.
whyNot.3: Respiratory infections are more common, but these tests are not routine syndrome checks.

B.q: A community learning disability nurse is planning how to detect dementia early in adults with Down syndrome. What does NICE NG54 recommend?
options: A baseline brain scan for every adult at the age of 40
Annual memory testing from 50 for those with symptoms
Genetic testing for APP gene copy number at diagnosis
A baseline of adaptive behaviour for all adults with Down syndrome
B.why: NICE NG54 1.7.13: carry out a baseline assessment of adaptive behaviour for all adults with Down's syndrome, so later change can be measured.

whyNot.0: Routine brain scans are not recommended for this purpose.
whyNot.1: Waiting for symptoms at 50 is too late to establish a baseline.
whyNot.2: Genetic testing for APP copy number is not part of NG54.

B.q: At the annual health check of Femi, 44, who has Down syndrome, his support worker describes several changes. Which one does NICE NG54 flag as possibly needing dementia assessment?
options: A gradual increase in his appetite and weight
Needing more prompting with tasks he did alone
More frequent colds over the winter months
Tiredness after a long day at his work placement
B.why: NICE NG54 1.5.4: ask about change in behaviour, loss of skills (including self-care) or a need for more prompting in recent months.

whyNot.0: Weight gain may suggest hypothyroidism or lifestyle factors, not the NG54 dementia prompt.
whyNot.2: More colds fits the infection risk, not dementia.
whyNot.3: Ordinary tiredness after work is not a loss of skills.

B.q: Kevin, 52, has Down syndrome. Staff notice brief, sudden jerks of his arms soon after he wakes, sometimes making him drop his cup. These are new. What is the most likely explanation?
options: A normal startle reaction in older adults
Possible seizures linked to emerging Alzheimer's
Behaviour to be recorded on an ABC chart
Muscle cramps from reduced daily activity
B.why: Late-onset (often myoclonic) epilepsy in Down syndrome is linked to Alzheimer's disease. New jerks need medical review.

whyNot.0: New jerks that make him drop things are not a normal startle.
whyNot.2: This is a possible neurological event, not behaviour to analyse.
whyNot.3: Cramps are sustained and painful, not brief jerks on waking.

C.q: Martin, 47, has Down syndrome. Over four months he has got lost on familiar routes, needs more prompting to shave and has lost interest in hobbies. His last thyroid test was 18 months ago. What should the nurse do first?
options: Refer him to the memory clinic for a dementia diagnosis
Increase staff prompts and record the change as ageing
Arrange thyroid tests and hearing and sight checks
Start a behaviour plan to address his withdrawal
C.why: Decline needs action, but treatable causes come first: hypothyroidism (overdue test), sensory loss and depression can mimic dementia. Then compare with his baseline and refer.

whyNot.0: Referral follows exclusion of treatable causes such as hypothyroidism.
whyNot.1: A loss of skills is not 'just ageing' and needs investigation.
whyNot.3: Withdrawal here may be illness; a behaviour plan risks diagnostic overshadowing.

C.q: Joanne, 36, has Down syndrome. Over three months she has become tired, feels cold, is constipated, has gained weight and is slower at her job. What is the most likely cause?
options: Early Alzheimer's disease, expected at her age
Hypothyroidism, which is common in Down syndrome
Low mood after a recent change of support staff
Heart failure from an undetected heart condition
C.why: Tiredness, feeling cold, constipation, weight gain and slowing together point to hypothyroidism, which is common and rises with age in Down syndrome.

whyNot.0: Dementia does not explain cold intolerance and constipation, and is usually diagnosed later.
whyNot.2: Low mood may cause slowing, but not cold intolerance and weight gain together.
whyNot.3: Heart failure presents with breathlessness and swelling, not this pattern.

C.q: A nurse is choosing a measure to track possible dementia in Paul, 44, who has Down syndrome. Which tool is named in NICE NG54 for this purpose?
options: The Glasgow Depression Scale
The DisDAT distress assessment tool
The AQ-10 autism screening questionnaire
The DSQIID dementia screening questionnaire
C.why: NICE NG54 1.7.12 names dementia measures including the DLD, DSDS and DSQIID (Dementia Screening Questionnaire for Individuals with Intellectual Disabilities).

whyNot.0: NG54 names the Glasgow Depression Scale for depression, not dementia.
whyNot.1: DisDAT documents distress cues; it is not a dementia measure.
whyNot.2: The AQ-10 screens for autism in adults without a moderate or severe learning disability.

reteach.title: Follow chromosome 21 through a life
reteach.question: If you followed a person with Down syndrome from birth to 60, at which points would you look for problems before they caused harm?

blocks.body: At birth: the heart. In childhood: hearing, sight, growth. Every year for life: the thyroid. In early adulthood: a baseline of skills. From the 30s: ask about change, because Alzheimer's arrives early. Through life: infections and the flu vaccine.

blocks.text: Before saying 'dementia', ask: thyroid? hearing? sight? mood? pain? medicines?

explain.body: An extra chromosome 21 (trisomy 21). About half of babies are born with a heart condition, and serious defects may not be obvious in the first days, so every baby has a heart assessment.

test.q: According to NHS.uk, about what proportion of babies with Down syndrome are born with a heart condition?
options: About one in ten
About a quarter
About three quarters
About half
test.why: NHS.uk: about half of all children with Down's syndrome are born with a heart condition.

explain.body: Hypothyroidism is common and risk rises with age. Test every year for life. It can mimic dementia or depression.

test.q: Dorothy, 45, has Down syndrome and has had normal thyroid results for twenty years. Her carer asks whether the yearly test can now stop. What is the best answer?
options: Test every five years now that results are stable
Keep testing every year, as the risk rises with age
Stop testing unless she develops symptoms
Test every two years from the age of 50
test.why: Thyroid testing continues every year for life because the risk of hypothyroidism rises with age.

whyNot.2: Symptoms are easily missed or mistaken for ageing; testing is routine.
whyNot.3: Testing stays yearly in later life.

explain.body: Hearing loss and glue ear, sight problems, and a weakened immune system with more chest infections and pneumonia. People with a learning disability are in the clinical risk groups for the annual flu vaccine.

test.q: Jamal, 7, has Down syndrome. His teacher says he often mishears instructions and has started talking more loudly. What should be checked first?
options: His hearing, as glue ear is common
His thyroid, as it affects attention
His vision, as squints are common
His behaviour, using an ABC chart
test.why: Hearing loss, including glue ear, is common in children with Down syndrome; mishearing and talking loudly point first to hearing.

whyNot.1: Thyroid problems matter, but these signs point to hearing.
whyNot.2: Sight problems would not explain mishearing.
whyNot.3: Assuming behaviour risks missing a treatable hearing problem.

explain.body: Extra APP gene: Alzheimer's changes by about 40, lifetime risk of dementia 90% or more. Early signs: behaviour or personality change, loss of skills, more prompting, late-onset seizures. Baseline for all adults (NG54 1.7.13); explain the link early to the person and family (NG96 1.5.36).

test.q: Kieran, 22, has Down syndrome. At his annual health check his father asks whether Down syndrome affects memory in later life. Which response follows NICE NG96?
options: Explain the dementia link now, accessibly, to them both
Reassure them it is not relevant until his forties
Discuss it with his father privately at a later date
Refer Kieran for a baseline brain scan at the memory clinic
test.why: NICE NG96 1.5.36: explain early to people with learning disabilities, particularly Down's syndrome, and their families about the link with dementia, in an accessible way.

whyNot.1: NG96 advises early explanation, not waiting.
whyNot.2: Kieran should be included, with accessible information.
whyNot.3: A baseline of adaptive behaviour is recommended, not a routine brain scan.
